paras: The threatened lynching of Houston Whiting took place in Charleston, West Virginia, in early May 1882, after Whiting, a Black barber, was accused of shooting a white man, T. S. Greaver, outside a saloon. While officers searched for him, papers reported threats to lynch him once caught, but he was arrested the next afternoon and no attack on him was reported.

Whiting, described as a mulatto barber of about twenty-four or twenty-five, had come to Charleston from Gallipolis, Ohio, and worked for the barbers Bullard & Robinson. Several papers said he had left Gallipolis to avoid arrest after cutting or stabbing a Black woman there. Greaver, a plasterer and former brakeman on the Chesapeake and Ohio railroad, lived in Huntington with his wife and children and had been working in Charleston for about a week.

About midnight on Monday, May 1, Greaver and friends were drinking in John Marley's saloon on Kanawha street after a circus when Whiting came in. According to the wire reports, Whiting asked Greaver to drink, was refused, and waited outside to shoot him. The Charleston papers instead said Whiting was drunk, aimed his revolver at another man, Bert Ong, after being pushed out the door, and then shot Greaver as he walked toward the entrance. Greaver, struck in the left breast, staggered back into the saloon and died within about half an hour.

Whiting fled, and Detective Burnett and the police went after him while the sheriff offered a $200 reward. A Pittsburg dispatch reported that a posse was in pursuit and that there were "threats of lynching Whiting when caught," and the Wheeling Intelligencer's correspondent wrote that "threats are uttered of dire vengeance." The Staunton Vindicator later said there had been "a strong feeling at Charleston for lynching him."

Whiting was arrested on the afternoon of May 2. The Kanawha Gazette reported that Morg. Stalmaker and Capt. R. W. Saunders found him hidden in Mon Handley's cellar on Quarrier street and collected the reward. A coroner's jury summoned by Justice Gates found that Greaver died of a pistol shot fired by Whiting. Greaver's body was taken to Staunton, Virginia, and buried there; no report of Whiting's trial or later fate appears in the coverage.

The National Associated Press wire ran on May 3 as "Killed For Refusing a Drink" in New Haven and under the headline "A Bad Coon" in Omaha, and the dispatch reporting the arrest appeared in Memphis and St. Paul the same day. A Maysville, Kentucky, news brief predicted that "the negro will be lynched."

Coverage in Virginia centered on Greaver as a Staunton native, with the Vindicator's account reprinted in the Richmond Dispatch. The Kanawha Gazette, reprinted in the Valley Virginian, called Whiting one of the "exquisite" darkies marked by "impudence" and anticipated his hanging, writing that his escape "now will be through a different trap door."

Accounts of the motive differed: the wire said Greaver had refused a drink, the Vindicator first quoted him as saying "You are not the kind I drink with," and the Charleston papers said Greaver was a stranger who had not spoken to Whiting. The Parkersburg West Virginia Freeman noted that reports were "conflicting as to the cause," and the Charleston accounts, written locally after the inquest, are the most detailed. The capture was also told two ways: in the Vindicator, Whiting was found under a house and tried to shoot the arresting officer, while the Kanawha Gazette credited two private men who found him in a cellar.

Whiting was not killed; the papers report only threats and a 'strong feeling' for lynching him over the shooting (A1, A3, A9), and he was arrested by officers or reward-seekers the next day (A4, A15).

The National Associated Press wire (A1, A2), the Wheeling special (A3), the Staunton Vindicator (A9) and the Maysville brevity (A8) all report lynching threats or expectations, and the arrest is reported by the Charleston AP dispatch and the Kanawha Gazette (A4, A15).

framing.detail: The National Associated Press wire ran as 'Killed For Refusing a Drink' in New Haven and as 'A Bad Coon' in Omaha, noting threats of lynching without comment.
The Wheeling Intelligencer headlined 'A Negro Barber Ruthlessly Shoots Down a White Man and Escapes' and reported threats of 'dire vengeance' as news.

The Kanawha Gazette called it 'An Unprovoked Murder', described Whiting with racial contempt and anticipated his hanging through 'a different trap door', implying legal execution rather than lynching.
